chapters.summary: Chair Joann Ariola introduces herself as chair of the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management and acknowledges Council Member Carmen De La Rosa and Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers. She states the hearing will examine emergency response in the Rockaways and other geographically isolated communities and frames the city's duty to provide prompt emergency services.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola opens hearing on emergency response in isolated communities

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I am Joanne Areola, and I am the chair to the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would like to acknowledge members of the committee who are here, Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa, and we are also joined by Councilmember Salvina Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Today's hearing will be an opportunity for the committee to examine emergency response in the Rockaways and other geographically isolated communities in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: A central component to a well-functioning city is a local government that prioritizes the prompt, effective, and efficient provision of emergency services to its residents.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As chair of the committee, we have routinely examined how the fire department and New York City emergency management and the city as a whole respond to emergency incidences.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Working to improve the city's delivery of emergency services, lower response times, and

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: expand access to life-saving protection and care that is offered by our first responders on each day.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As a lifelong resident of Queens, I take pride in representing the interests of the city's out-of-borough residents and have worked tirelessly to ensure the vital city services are provided equally to New Yorkers throughout the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Given the geographic expanse of our city, responding to emergency incidences are far-reaching neighborhoods of our outer boroughs can present challenges

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: for first responders and other city entities that provide support services at the scene of emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Today, we plan to examine how the city responds to emergencies in geographically remote areas.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We will look at how first responders are deployed and stationed to ensure prompt emergency responses and how the city ensures all New Yorkers receive emergency services promptly, regardless of where they live.

chapters.summary: Ariola says the hearing will highlight a summer emergency in Far Rockaway in Council Member Brooks-Powers's district, where two people died and families were displaced. She thanks public attendees and administration witnesses, including NYCEM Commissioner Christina Farrell, FDNY EMS Chief Paul Maiano, and Assistant Chief John Sirocco.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola announces July 25 Far Rockaway incident and thanks agency witnesses

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Today's hearing will highlight an emergency incident that occurred this summer in Far Rockaway, Queens, in Councilmember Brooks Powers'district.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Powers will further speak about what happened in her community and what her constituents experienced in the city's response.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But I hope that we can use exploring this incident as a hands-on opportunity to work collaboratively to improve the city's function.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would also like to thank those from the public as well as representatives from the administration, Commissioner Christina Farrell from New York City Emergency Management, Chief John Sirocco from

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: FDNY EMS, and Chief Paul Maiano from FDNY EMS.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You're here to provide information.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sam Salam has also joined us.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is he?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: He's on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: as far as we go.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So at this point, I would like to defer to my colleague, Councilmember Brooks Powers, for her statement.

chapters.summary: Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers thanks the Chair and Speaker for convening the hearing and notes increasing weather events affecting coastal communities. She describes the July 25 incident in Far Rockaway, where two people died and families were displaced while a major Bronx fire also strained resources.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers describes July 25 Far Rockaway fire and scattered response

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Areola, and I will keep it brief so that we can get into the heart of the questions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'd like to first thank you, Chair, as well as the Speaker, for quickly responding to the needs of my community and convening an important hearing such as this.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As New York has seen much more regularly, there have been a number of weather events that have been happening, impacting communities, particularly coastal communities that have always been frontline, but even more inland.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what sparked this particular request was the July 25th incident that happened where we saw two deaths.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We had a number of families that were impacted, and the response felt very scattered and the resources very bare.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And at that...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Time there was also a massive fire happening in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And while we don't control when emergencies happen and where they happen, it

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: raised the concern once again in terms of what type of resources exist for geographically isolated communities such as the Rockaways.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers praises FDNY and EMTs but worries they must rely on mainland resources to reach the Rockaways. She questions whether Red Cross services are sufficient for displaced families and hopes the hearing will identify gaps that lead to internal reforms or Council legislation.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers calls for identifying gaps in isolated-community emergency response

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I, the EMTs, they have been tremendous to my community and their service to us.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And quite frankly, I worry about them when they have to respond also to these crises because we depend on mainland resources to be able to get to us.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When we talk about Red Cross and what services they provide, I think we need to revisit what, quite frankly, is sufficient in moments like this where we have.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Dozens of families that end up being displaced, and just being able to respond much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so I hope in the questions today we're able to identify where some of the gaps may be that could spark either internal reform within these agencies and response

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: divisions or prompt legislation on the council side to be able to provide the direction that may be needed.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So again, I thank you for the opportunity, Chair, to bring this important conversation to the public.

chapters.summary: NYCEM Commissioner Christina Farrell introduces herself and her colleagues, Chief of EMS Paul Maiano and Assistant Chief of Fire Operations John Sirocco. She notes it is the final day of National Preparedness Month and says the Emergency Operations Center has been activated for 183 days and the Flash Flood Plan for 90 days so far this year.
chapters.title: Commissioner Farrell begins testimony on 2026 emergency activations

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Good morning, Chief Areola and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I'm Christina Farrell, Commissioner of New York City Emergency Management, and as has been noted, I am joined today by Chief of EMS, Paul Maiano, and Assistant Chief of Fire Operations, John Sirocco.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: It is our pleasure to be here today on the final day of National Preparedness Month to testify on the topic of emergency response in the Rockaways and other geographically isolated communities in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: As you all know, this has been an exceptionally busy year for activations.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So far this year, the Emergency Operations Center has been activated for 183 days and the Flash Flood Plan for 90 days.

chapters.summary: Farrell describes the recent nor'easter that brought heavy rain, wind, and flooding to the Rockaways, Arverne, and Howard Beach. She lists NYCEM actions, including tracking the storm for four days, activating the Flash Flood Plan early, sending Notify NYC messages, monitoring flood sensors, and distributing flood barrier and pump kits.
chapters.title: Farrell details nor'easter response and flood outreach

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: This past weekend brought a nor'easter and associated heavy rains, wind gusts, and flooding into isolated communities such as the Rockaways, Arvern, and Howard Beach.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Emergency management tracked this weather system for four days before the first raindrop fell, activated the flash flood plan early, and scaled operations as the forecast worsened.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: During this time, we held two elected official calls, monitored 400...

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: 50 flood sensors in real time, sent 32 Notify NYC messages, worked with 39 strengthening community partners to reach more than 200,000 people

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: in 12 languages, and received more than 1.8 million social media views and impressions.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Notify NYC now has more than 1.65 million subscribers, with 22,000 added just this weekend and more than 234,000 added since the start of the year.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Enrollment in our basement apartments alerts has grown nearly 30% this year to more than 8,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Our Instagram has grown by 38% this year with over 5,000 new followers this past week.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: This weekend, we delivered 51 flood barriers kits and 24 pump kits to residents in the Rockaways and Howard Beach.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: The Downtree Task Force was activated and received close to 2,700 requests.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And much of the City Council was directly active with me and with our team through the duration of the emergency.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: As always, we thank you for your partnership and your assistance.

chapters.summary: Farrell notes the year's long cold snap and extreme July heat, and reminds the committee that hurricane season continues. She says geographic isolation is central to hurricane evacuation zones, which is why the entire Rockaways Peninsula is classified as Zone 1 along with places like Roosevelt Island, City Island, and Coney Island.
chapters.title: Farrell explains hurricane evacuation zones for geographically isolated areas

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: This year, we also saw the second longest cold snap in the city's history, followed by some of the hottest temperatures and heat indices in the city's history during the July 4th holiday.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: As you know, we are still in hurricane season.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Geographic isolation is a central factor in designing our hurricane evacuation zones.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: For example, while the entire Rockaways Peninsula may not be completely inundated by storm surge, we classify the entire area as Zone 1.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: The isolation and limited access routes lead us to treat these areas as special cases to ensure residents remain safe, even if not directly impacted by a particular hazard.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: There are similar considerations taken into effect for other geographically isolated areas of the city, such as Roosevelt Island, City Island, Coney Island, and parts of Staten Island.

chapters.summary: Farrell describes how NYCEM supports residents forced from their homes by fire, flood, or structural issues, often by opening a school or dispatching an MTA bus for sheltering and Red Cross registration. She lists triggers for NYCEM response, including sensitive-location one-alarm fires, two-alarm residential fires, three-alarm fires, fires with two or more fatalities, and fires requiring interagency coordination.
chapters.title: Farrell outlines sheltering and fire response triggers

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: One of the most heartbreaking incidents that city agencies respond to are incidents when New Yorkers are forced to leave their homes, whether the result of a fire, flood, or structural issues.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: During larger incidents, like multi-alarm fires or large vacates, emergency management will respond and support immediate sheltering of residents.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Often this involves opening a nearby public school or dispatching an MTA bus where residents can remain out of the elements and register for services with the Red Cross, including a hotel placement.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Emergency management.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: uses triggers and protocols to respond to requests for sheltering assistance.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: These were developed to ensure we respond to incidents with a need for interagency coordination on scene based on the likelihood of a multi-agency response and the complexity of these types of incidents.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: While the majority of fire calls are handled locally by FDNY resources, we respond to the following.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: One alarm fires in a sensitive location, such as schools, houses of worship, or city properties.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Two alarm fires in residential properties.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Three alarm fires and above.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Any fire with two or more fatalities, any fire where we have been requested by FDNY, buildings, NYPD, or any other agency to provide interagency coordination at the scene.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: These fires usually involve requests for utility shutoffs or repairs or overcrowding and squatting conditions.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Emergency management citywide incident coordinators will also lead on-scene meetings with relevant agencies and landlords to identify immediately needed resources, such as large-scale equipment or food and water,

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: and any need for additional public messaging.

chapters.summary: Farrell says the Red Cross monitors public safety communications and responds to fires at one alarm and above, and NYCEM notifies the Red Cross when a fire is likely to displace residents. Displaced residents are registered and placed in a hotel for two nights, then referred to HPD for longer-term shelter case management if eligible.
chapters.title: Farrell explains Red Cross hotel placement and HPD referrals

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: In addition to our city resources, the Red Cross monitors public safety communications and responds to all fires that reach one alarm and above.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: On a daily basis, the Red Cross responds to vacate situations across the city to register New Yorkers and provide them with temporary hotel placement.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Additionally, if emergency management responds to a fire that is likely to displace residents, we will notify the Red Cross to ensure they are also responding.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Once registered with them, displaced residents are placed in a hotel for two nights.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Residents are then referred to HPD for longer-term case management assistance if they qualify for the HPD shelter system.

chapters.summary: Farrell describes NYCEM's Strengthening Communities grants for community preparedness networks, noting the Far Rockaway Arverne Nonprofit Coalition has participated since 2021. She also says CERT expanded with a Far Rockaway training that added 39 volunteers, and CERT members are canvassing at-risk neighborhoods through October.
chapters.title: Farrell highlights Strengthening Communities and CERT programs

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Emergencies and disasters can strike at any moment, which is why emergency management is proud to offer several programs to help New Yorkers readiness and resilience.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: The Strengthening Communities program offers grants to community networks to build their emergency preparedness plan and provide information to their neighbors during

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: time of emergency.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: These networks were activated during winter weather and extreme heat and play a significant role in flood preparedness.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: The Far Rockaway Arvern Nonprofit Coalition, or FRANK, has been part of Strengthening Communities since the program launched in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Frank provides various community programs and youth development programs within Far Rockaway and has connections with faith-based congregations throughout the community.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We will have an open application in October for additional networks throughout the city, and we'll work with the council to help amplify this opportunity when these applications open.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Additionally, Emergency Management recently expanded its Community Emergency Response Team, or CERT, program by delivering a local basic training in Far Rockaway,

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: adding 39 community residents to a volunteer corps of more than 640 members citywide.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Since its launch in 2003,

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: New York City CERT has grown to 24 divisions covering all 59 community boards, and it remains a critical resource in supporting New York City during and after disasters.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Building on that momentum, CERT members are conducting community canvassing through the end of October to share preparedness tips on coastal storms and flooding with residents in at-risk neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Emergencies affect every community differently, but we work with all communities to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We want to thank the council as well for helping us with these measures.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: from amplifying our messaging to being cooling center partners to helping us distribute masks during air quality alert days to being active with CERT.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We greatly appreciate your partnership and assistance.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the council and we are happy to answer your questions.

chapters.summary: Chair Ariola thanks Farrell for coordinating the nor'easter response and acknowledges Council Members Maloney and Sanchez. She asks whether NYCEM developed guidance under Local Law 60 for safe evacuation before flash flooding, and Farrell describes Red Cross call-downs and overnight safe locations opened in schools during summer flooding.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola asks Farrell about Local Law 60 flash flood evacuation guidance

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner, and thank you for the coordination over this nor'easter in my district and in the coastal districts.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You really did an amazing job of putting together all the other agencies and making sure that everyone was safe.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And informed and the public was informed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So we really thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Just would like to mention that we have been joined by council members Maloney and Pierina Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I am going to ask two questions regarding legislation and I'm going to yield to council member Brooks Powers because I know she has some questions specific to the Rockaway Peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So for NYSIM, with regard to Local Law 60 of 2025, NYSIM is required to develop guidance for facilitating safe evacuation before flash flooding emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Has this guidance been developed?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if so, can you please describe the specifics for the committee?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Yes, so we definitely have guidance.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We happily this past weekend did not result in an evacuation situation, but, you know, nor we stirs can.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: In addition, we have had several, as everyone knows, flash flooding events over the summer.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so we have worked with our partners.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: As we do our coordination, as you mentioned, we do things like a Red Cross call down in case we do need to look for hotel rooms.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We also partner, people may have seen over the summer, three times we opened

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: safe overnight locations in 51 schools, one in each district, in case people that live in basement apartments or in low-lying area need a place to go.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Several residents took us up on that, and that is something that we are codifying further.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether FDNY posted QR codes on vehicles to distribute residential fire emergency response guides under Local Law 134 and what percentage of the fleet is complete. Assistant Chief John Sirocco says FDNY began posting QR codes on fire apparatus over the past year and that all fire-operation vehicles involved in fire response have them.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola asks FDNY about Local Law 134 QR codes on fire vehicles

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And for the FDMY, with regard to Local Law 134 of 2025, the law

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: also requires FDMY to distribute the guide at the scene of residential fires using a quick response or QR code posted on FDMY vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Has the QR code been posted on the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if so, how many or the percentage of the fleet have been completed or started?

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Yeah, we have posted QR codes as far as the data is the amount.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: I don't have that information, but we have started that process a while ago over the last year of posting QR codes on a fire apparatus.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So victims of fires can scan it and get information regarding the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: All vehicles that are involved in fire response have them.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So all the vehicles in the fire department on the fire operation side does have QR codes on their apparatus.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Council Member Brooks-Powers asks Commissioner Farrell to recount the July 25 Far Rockaway fire and alleged double homicide from the 911 call until the last displaced family had a bed. Farrell says NYCEM did not initially respond, later sent a citywide incident coordinator after outreach from the Council Member's office, and the Red Cross registered and placed residents in hotels that evening.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks Farrell to walk through July 25 response timeline

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Council member?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And just echoing the Chair, definitely want to thank you, Commissioner, for being so responsive to my text messages throughout the Northeaster.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So, as I mentioned before, on July 25th, there was...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: An alleged double homicide and fire in Far Rockaway, Queens.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Surrounding homes were evacuated and families were displaced.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you walk us through July 25th from the 911 call moment to the moment the last displaced family had a bed that night?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just wanting to know, like, for example, what time NISM was actually activated and notified and what resources arrived in response to that.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So we were made aware of the fire but did not initially respond, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Then as the situation evolved, as many of these situations do, later that evening there was outreach to us, I believe, initiated by your office and others in the community.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so we did send one of our season's citywide incident coordinators out there, you know, to get an update on what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, once he got situational awareness, it was indeed.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know he determined that the Red Cross should be there It's my understanding that the Red Cross was dispatched earlier since it was an active crime scene and there were other things going on They were not

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: able to access the property earlier in the day, but Red Cross did come that evening and they Did begin to register?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Folks there were I think the power had been cut and some other things so they registered some people in surrounding properties there were also a couple of residents that I understand had

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: relocated temporarily to Staten Island or other places and so they tracked them down and saw what assistance they needed and got people into hotels that evening

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many households and individuals were displaced and where they spent their first night. Farrell says she lacks specific hotel information but understands 22 adults and seven children, representing multiple households, received temporary lodging through the Red Cross; Brooks-Powers notes there were also pets.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks how many residents were displaced on July 25

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to a part of this that I'd like to unpack a bit more.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But can you tell me how many households and individuals were displaced and where did each spend their first night?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I don't have specific information, you know, things like specific hotels and things are kept private.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The geography is fine, like you said, somewhere in Staten Island, for example.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But how many families were displaced?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: My understanding is that 22 adults and seven children, obviously representing multiple households, received temporary lodging through the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And there were a few animals, too.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I don't have that information, but often there are pets that Red Cross works to find pet-friendly hotels.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether NYCEM or City Hall was made aware that the July 25 incident involved a shooting with multiple injuries or deaths. Farrell says one-alarm fires are not routinely deployed to unless in a sensitive location, and Brooks-Powers describes a disconnect between the mayor's press conference and the on-the-ground response felt by residents.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers questions whether City Hall knew about the shooting

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Now, when the 911 call came in and the initial response happened,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Was NYSOM or City Hall made aware that it was not only a fire, but that there was a shooting that took place with multiple people injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So one alarm fires, unless, like I said at the beginning, unless it's a sensitive location, we don't routinely...

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Deploy to those.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, our watch command is 24-7.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: This was a Saturday, right?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: were working, they will definitely give a, what we call a monitor page to myself and other members on call of the executive team so we know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: But the actual initial response and what was going on with PD and fire, we were not part of that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Yeah, because I was wondering the disconnect because earlier in the day, I believe the mayor had a press conference and he acknowledged what was happening in Rockaway.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But on the ground, we didn't feel the response.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Obviously, FDNY and PD were there.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But in terms of like an effort to address the.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The crisis in that moment on the ground at the magnitude that was felt by the people impacted, that was not present.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers describes a mother and five children trapped upstairs during the active crime scene, stepping over blood and bodies, and says the constituent still feels unsupported. She asks what resources exist for trauma and what the city's responsibility is; Farrell says Red Cross can provide mental health counseling but NYCEM usually focuses on utilities and will identify the right follow-up agency.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers describes constituent trauma and asks about mental health resources

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know there was a family, there's a mom with five children who lived upstairs in that house, and they felt...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Quite honestly, and were hostages because, of course, it's a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: No one knows who's who at that initial moment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so for a very long time, her and her kids were pretty much not permitted to leave their apartment upstairs, having to step over.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Blood and dead bodies thereafter.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And to this day, that constituent has felt like there has not been enough done for her and her family in terms of dealing with the trauma.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: or treating them as the victims of what transpired there that had nothing to do with her or her family.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What, I guess, resources are in play for moments like this?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what is the city's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I will have to get, so obviously at the beginning it was a police investigation, and then as you mentioned, I know that when Red Cross does get involved, you know, they do.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Do some mental health counseling and look at things like that.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, any type of impacted resident services and things, those are not things that emergency management is usually involved in as we're focused on, you know, the utilities and all of those pieces.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, obviously the trauma and the things that come along with this are serious and life-changing, as you said.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So we can go back and look exactly who the right person is to follow up on that question.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'd appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what triggers notifications to Red Cross, HPD, the Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery, and DSS after a fire with displacement and who sends them. Farrell explains that NYCEM has limited staffing, that Red Cross notification would normally go through HPD, and that NYCEM makes additional notifications when its citywide incident coordinators respond.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks about notification protocols after a displacing fire

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In terms of communication and follow-up, that was a good segue.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is the protocol for notifying the other agencies and partners involved in recovery?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So like the Red Cross, HPD, the Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery, Department of Social Services, and others after a fire with displacement and what triggers each notification and who sends it?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So if it's a larger, and as you noted, there was a large, another large fire going on, I think almost at the same time,

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: which, you know, many of our resources we have, as you probably know, were a lot smaller than our partners at FDNY, NYPD, and others.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: On a typical Saturday afternoon, we probably had three citywide incident coordinators working, also doing things like monitoring the drones at the beaches and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So, you know, we have limited resources, just nature of the way we're set up across the agency.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Since we did not initially respond to this fire, the Red Cross notification, as I said, they did initially respond.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: That would go through housing preservation and development.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Once things were needed later on, when our CIC went out there, that's when we would do those notifications.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: If it's something that we initially respond to, say like a three alarm fire or more, those notifications and the requests, you know, Councilwoman Sanchez knows there was a significant fire in her district a week ago

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: and buildings was requested, Con Ed was requested, HPD.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Mayor's Office of Engagement.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So depending on the number of units, you know, the likelihood

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: that there is going to be a vacate, we will pull in our partners.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says Red Cross could not take certain directives from NYPD because the scene was a crime scene and asks whether communication should run through NYCEM. Farrell explains the HPD-Red Cross contract covers vacates from fires, power outages, and water outages, not primarily police scenes, and says Red Cross housed families using private funding in this case.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers and Farrell discuss Red Cross contract limits and communication gaps

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: To that point, because I know in talking to Red Cross that night, there were certain decisions that they couldn't make unless it came from HPD, for example.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if through NISM they communicate because it's an emergency there or if the regular channels have to kind of communicate during normal business hours.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Per se, in the sense of making certain calls.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So like, in their mind, the fire has been handled, they can go into their home.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But then it was an active crime scene, and so they could not go back into their home.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But there was a disconnect with Red Cross, and they could not take that directive from NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you feel that there should be a different, I guess, communication stream in moments like this, where maybe it runs through NYSIM, since you're connecting all the agencies in these moments of crisis?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So the contract with HPD and Red Cross is for vacates and usually outside of the fire investigation, which can, of course, result in criminality.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Usually these vacates that they respond to and that they put people into hotels, they're based on

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: you know, fires that make a house uninhabitable or an apartment building, things like extended power outages and water service outages through a water main break or other situations.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So this situation, as we've mentioned, was different in that

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, it was primarily a police scene, and that is not what this contract is set up for.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Red Cross was able to house these families.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: They didn't do it through the HPD contract.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: It's my understanding that they had other funding, private funding that they used, that they can use unlimited.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: occasions.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: But this is really a different type of incident than what the Red Cross contract is set up for, which is more, you know, the typical fires and the things that come with those vacates.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because also the power was out.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so in terms of the connection from PSEG, that communication to HPD, to Red Cross, that communication tree wasn't happening either.

chapters.summary: Farrell says the city can always communicate better and announces that NYCEM received city tax levy funding in July for 10 additional citywide incident coordinators and five part-time coordinators. She says the added resources will help but does not promise NYCEM can respond to every incident.
chapters.title: Farrell announces funding for additional citywide incident coordinators

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So, I mean, I think, you know, we can always do a better job of communicating.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, one thing I am happy to say is that.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We actually in July received funding for

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: 10 additional citywide incident coordinators, city tax levy funding, and for five part-time citywide incident coordinators because we do have people that are retired and would like to come back.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so that will greatly increase our resources because, again, if we have three people working citywide,

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, that gets very, you know, they get very busy very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So we are excited to have these additional resources.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And then as they are in place, we could potentially explore.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: But I don't want to promise that we can be involved in every one of these incidents when we are really coordinating for those larger incidents.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers yields back to Chair Ariola, who asks how FDNY responds when a fire may also involve a crime scene. Sirocco says FDNY responds with caution, requests NYPD simultaneously, and dispatchers notify NYPD when they know there is a shooting or shooter.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola asks FDNY protocol for a fire that is also a crime scene

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to yield.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I have a few more questions, but I'm yielding to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So it's interesting because we're talking about a fire that then became a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So for the FDMY, what is the FDMY protocol to respond to a fire when it may also involve a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Well, when we respond, then we are aware from the discipline.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: There may be a shooting there.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: We respond with caution.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: But we still respond and we're there to put that fire out.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So we don't want to put our people in undue danger.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: But in those situations, we would respond with caution and we would request NYPD response to that location along with us.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So there's a coordination between NYPD, NYSOM, and FDMY.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: We would, in that situation, when our dispatchers know there is a shooter or shooting, they will notify NYPD simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, wonderful.

chapters.summary: Ariola acknowledges Council Member Paladino and NYU students, then asks how FDNY explains geographic disparities in response times in areas like Breezy Point and the Rockaway Peninsula. Sirocco says Rockaways response times are good, with the 4-7 Battalion ranking well, and describes six engines, three trucks, a bushfire unit, water rescue training, summer boat patrols, and must-fill units.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola asks FDNY about response times in isolated communities

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to make note that Councilmember Palladino has joined us, and also we're joined by students from NYU.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We welcome you to the hearing, and we're glad that you're interested to come and view and see what goes on here.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You'll see council members coming and going from this hearing because there are other hearings going on that they are members of those committees as well.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I just want to, and if you have any questions, happy to answer them after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But I'm very glad that you're showing an interest.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Data from the city reflects geographic disparities in emergency response times, specifically in isolated communities, showing longer response times in areas such as Breezy Point and the Rockaway Peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: My question is, how does the department, fire department, explain such dramatic changes in response times in certain areas?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: neighborhoods as opposed to others?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And what is the department doing to address this issue?

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: My data shows that in the Rockaways we respond pretty well.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: The 4-7 Battalion is the battalion that's in the Rockaways, and there's only five battalions out of the 49 that respond quicker.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: On the peninsula, we have six units and six engines and three trucks, including we do put in service at BFU.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Which is a bushfire unit.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Those units are all water rescue trained.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: We do in the summertime also put a summer boat program in play where we patrol the beach with that and also drones.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: In my view, we respond pretty well to the Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Those units are all must-fill units.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So, for example, if somebody's out for training in the Rockaways, we replace them with another unit.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So it's always covered because of its isolation.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So I think we do overall on the fire ops side an excellent job of covering that peninsula.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: My data shows our response times are pretty good in the Rockaways.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks about EMS response. Chief Paul Maiano says EMS response times in the Rockaways are lower than the citywide average, with a station co-located with an engine company housing 10 EMS units, including seven BLS, three ALS, and two hazmat ambulances, plus summer gator units and drone coordination.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola asks EMS about Rockaways response times and resources

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right, so that's with fire response.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: What about EMS response?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So similarly for EMS, our response times are lower than the average citywide response times in the Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We do have one station on the Rockaways that's co-located.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: with an engine company.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: It houses 10 units, 10 EMS units.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: Seven of them are BLS units.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: Three of them are advanced life support units.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: And of those 10 units, two of them are also members of our Special Operations Command.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: They're hazardous materials ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: Also during the summer, we put out two gator units on the beaches in the Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We work very closely with the fire department's drone unit on those beaches to be able to respond quicker.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks for the current EMS headcount and how it has changed. Maiano says EMS is approximately 400 members below headcount, meaning fewer ambulances on the street, but the Central Resource Coordination Center moves ambulances from high-availability areas to low-availability areas to maintain response times.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola asks EMS headcount and impact on response times

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And sticking with EMS, what is the current head count for EMS?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How has it increased or decreased over the past few years?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And how has that impacted response times?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: The current headcount for EMS, the exact number, I don't have written down, but I can tell you that we are below headcount of approximately 400 members.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: In regards to response times, that does mean less ambulances on the street.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: However,

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We have what we call the Central Resource Coordination Center, and that is a 24-hour staff center that consistently looks at ambulance availability throughout the city and deploys ambulances from areas that

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: have a large amount of availability into areas that have reduced availability so we can maintain our response times.

chapters.summary: Ariola describes a 14-year-old cardiac patient at St. Francis Preparatory who showed stroke symptoms on September 28; the nurse and parents called 911 multiple times starting at 8:47 a.m. She says no ambulance responded, and the mother eventually drove the child to the hospital without paramedics.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola details September 28 student stroke and delayed ambulance

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I want to talk about a specific incident that happened on Monday, September 28th.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: A 14-year-old young man, student at St.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Francis Preparatory High School, started to show signs of a stroke almost immediately upon entering school.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: He's slurring his words.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: His right and left eye began to droop, his right eye and arm.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And leg became weak and unstable.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This student is a known cardiac patient.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The nurse immediately called 911.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The first call to 911 was made at 8.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The second call was made at 9.14 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And the third call was made at 9.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As the parents rushed to the school upon hearing that FDNY had not yet responded with an ambulance, the child's father called

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: 911 also at 9.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Still no ambulance responded.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The mother arrived at the school at 9.22.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And calls were made.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: When after five minutes, there was still no response, she took the child and rushed him to the hospital in her own car without a paramedic, without an EMT treating her severely ill child.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Why did the FDNY not respond to these frantic calls for help?

chapters.summary: Maiano calls the situation tragic and says EMS was experiencing a surge of 274 calls in that hour, about 100 above normal. He says an ambulance was dispatched from a distance and arrived at 9:37 a.m., about five minutes after the parents had already driven the child to the hospital.
chapters.title: Maiano explains call surge and ambulance arrival after parents left

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So first off, I just want to say that this is an extremely tragic situation.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: I am a father myself of three boys, and I could not imagine what those parents were going through at the school.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: What I can tell you is at the time that this call was coming in, EMS was experiencing a 100-plus call surge than what we normally see.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We normally see about 179 calls per hour.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: And during this hour that this assignment took place, we had a call volume of 274 calls for service into 911.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: An ambulance was dispatched to this call.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: The ambulance was coming from a distance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: They did arrive at the location, but they did arrive after the parents left to take the child to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How long after?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: They actually arrived at 9.37, and it's believed that the child left to go to the hospital five minutes prior to that.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether the delay was due to staffing or a dispatcher shortage. Maiano explains that 911 calls initially go to NYPD dispatchers and are transferred to EMS; when no EMS alarm receiving dispatcher is available, NYPD stays on the line and routes the call, while the system continuously searched for an available ambulance.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about dispatcher disconnect; Maiano explains call routing

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you were holding about 274 calls, right, which is above the norm.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We received 274 calls, which was about 100 above the normal at that time during the day.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And do you think that the disconnect was because it was due to a lack of staffing or an EMS dispatcher was not available to speak to the caller?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So when someone calls 911, they initially talk to a police dispatcher.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: That police dispatcher.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: or ask questions, police, fire, EMS.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: When it is determined that it is a request for EMS service, it is transferred from NYPD to EMS.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: When there are no EMS alarm receiving dispatchers available, the NYPD dispatcher stays on the line, takes additional information, and then routes that call to EMS.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So the call itself is not lingering.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: It is in the EMS system.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: The system did, throughout this whole period of time, note that it was searching for ambulances, searching for ambulances, searching for ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: But due to the surge in calls that we had at that time, we had none available.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: As soon as an ambulance became available, the system alerted the radio dispatcher, who then dispatched the ambulance to the location.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: And like I said, they were coming from a distance, and they did arrive at the scene.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: But unfortunately, it was after the parent had left.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether 911 told callers that an ambulance was delayed or gave an estimated wait. Maiano says there is no system in place to advise callers of extended delays.
chapters.title: Ariola asks whether 911 notified callers of the ambulance delay

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And was there any notification back from 911 to the people who called saying, you know, there is a delay, we're holding, you know, we got an influx of calls,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: it'll be a matter of 15, 20, 25 minutes before an ambulance gets there.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Was that done?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: No, so there is no system in place where we advise the caller that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: That there is a, you know, that an ambulance is delayed or will be an extended period of time before they arrive.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether the child was entered as an unknown condition rather than a level one. Maiano confirms it went in as unknown because it did not reach an EMS dispatcher for triage; he says EMS dispatch was adequately staffed with 26 alarm receiving dispatchers, and proper triage likely would have classified it around segment three rather than segment four.
chapters.title: Ariola questions why stroke call was triaged as unknown

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So basically what you're saying is that a child who is a cardiac patient showing signs of a stroke was put into a system as an unknown condition.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is that how it went into the system?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: That's how it went into the system.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And instead of a level one, which is the most serious of conditions, as it should have been coded,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: because of the lack of staffing for EMS and for the dispatchers at that moment, it was not put in as a level one.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams thanks the Chair and committee and lists isolated neighborhoods including parts of Staten Island, City Island, Howard Beach, Broad Channel, Red Hook, and the Rockaways. utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Certain New York City neighborhoods that are geographically isolated, including parts of Staten Island, City Island, Howard Beach, Broad Channel, Red Hook, and the Rockaways, face heightened overlapping risks during climate emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Many of these areas'vulnerabilities stem largely from structural limitations or critical infrastructure needs.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: These communities face frontline climate exposures, meaning that they tend to bear the brunt of coastal storms and may rely on single bridges or narrow causeways for emergency access.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Severe weather events in New York City, such as the late September 2026 nor'easter, have routinely triggered localized flooding up to three feet, causing power disruptions and trapping residents who rely on local utilities like Con Edison.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Though geography impacts transit in many cities, data tracked by New York City's Emergency Management, NYSIM, and the New York City Fire Department, FDNY, show that traffic density, staffing shortages, and high call volumes inflate response times for

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: far more than just physical distance.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Furthermore, the events of August 2026 demonstrated the city's vulnerability to widespread emergency system failures, revealing how whole disruptions to 9-11 call services can occur.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Although the city has taken steps to safeguard local businesses and residents against the escalating impacts of climate change, further action is absolutely necessary to enhance our emergency response frameworks to ensure priority assistance reaches geographically isolated communities.

chapters.summary: Williams says MTA and NYCEM pre-stage diesel locomotives, high-water rescue vehicles, and pumps in isolated zones, but these areas are not routinely designated as emergency corridors. He recalls Hurricane Sandy recovery, $14 billion in federal aid, public housing disruptions, and argues the city needs a resilient long-term emergency response strategy that does not depend on federal aid.
chapters.title: Williams urges emergency corridors and long-term Sandy recovery strategy

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In order to mitigate transit, transit.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: issues during extreme weather events, the MTA and NYSEN pre-staged diesel locomotives, high water, rescue vehicles, and utility pumps inside isolated zones before storms make landfall to keep emergency corridors operational.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Yet, because isolated areas are not routinely designated or integrated as emergency corridors, local residents and businesses cannot often find

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: can often find themselves trapped, unable to evacuate, or effectively combat incoming very forceful winds and rising floodwaters.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As many of us have learned over the recent years, severe weather conditions cause widespread damages to all types of personal properties.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Following Hurricane Sandy in 2012, New York City received more than

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: $14 billion in federal aid to fund various municipal initiatives and recovery projects, a number of which remain active today to support households, commercial entities, and damaged infrastructures.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The aftermath of Hurricane Sandy underscores the critical necessity of establishing a resilient long-term emergency response strategy specifically designed for New York City's geographically isolated neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: During the storm, public housing suffered severe disruption as floodwaters impacted 10% of NITRA developments, leaving nearly 400 buildings without electricity, heat, or hot water.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In the years following Sandy, New York has confronted the reality that reliance on federal aid may not always be dependable, particularly amid disagreements with the Trump administration.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Consequently, it is vital that we actively collaborate to devise innovative solutions that safeguard our coastal areas and shorelines.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This approach ensures we maintain our standing as a global hub while advancing key local initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: initiatives, including the revitalization of city waterways and working ports such as the Hunts Point Marine Terminal in the Bronx and the Brooklyn Marine Terminal in Red Hook.
