chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says she was deeply disappointed with the Red Cross on July 25, when it left and returned after 11 p.m., partly because it lacked resources and had to travel over an hour from the Bronx. She asks whether the city has a backup to Red Cross or could revisit its contract when Red Cross lacks capacity.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers criticizes Red Cross response and asks about backup capacity

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And going back to Red Cross, because I will say I was deeply disappointed with the Red Cross that day.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And that was not the first time in a moment of crisis.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I know that they are contract bound in some instances.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So really just wanting to know.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: if an agreement could be put in place, whether it's through NISM or HPD, when Red Cross does not have the bandwidth and capacity, who then comes in?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because when we called that night to have them come back, because you're right, they came earlier, they left, they didn't really do any triage, but they did when they came back after 11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That night.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And the reason it came so late was, one, the fire was going on.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They had no more resources to send to us.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then geographically, it takes over an hour to get from the part of the Bronx they were to the part of Far Rockaway they needed to get to.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Does the city currently have a backup to the Red Cross, or is this something we could explore to having a backup or revisiting what their contract entails?

chapters.summary: Farrell says NYCEM borough-deploys coordinators based on likely hazards, and during the nor'easter its Queens coordinator worked in Brooks-Powers's neighborhoods. On Red Cross, she says the contract focuses on hotel placement, and when hotel demand outstrips supply, the city can set up congregate shelters in schools or other facilities.
chapters.title: Farrell explains borough deployment, Red Cross hoteling, and congregate shelters

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So I will just say two things.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: On your earlier point, you know, when we, BUR, deploy our CICs, we look at where the most likely hazards are.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So, for example, this weekend, our CIC that was working in Queens was in your neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Far Rock, you know, driving, working within that area.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So we do do that based on, you know, as we see things coming in.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: With respect to the Red Cross, you know, that contract is one where we look at hoteling.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And I'm sure you both are familiar because it is.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: It has happened during different times.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: If there are not, because a lot of what they do is also based on the hotel room availability, you know, sometimes are busier than others.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: The summer obviously was very busy.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Last week was busy with United Nations General Assembly and Climate Week.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so if what's needed to house people, if the demand outstrips the supply, we then look at congregate sheltering, which means

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: setting up a shelter in a most likely a school building or another facility like that.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So that is what we do when we don't have the resources available.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: But just like, you know, with the Red Cross, we are always looking at ways.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And, you know, by and large, you probably know their model is based on volunteers responding to many of their incidents 24-7.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so they really do a fantastic job getting to all of these scenes.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: But it's a very large city.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: There are a lot of incidents that come.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And I know this is one they're specifically looking at to see how they can improve response.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says the committee must raise the need for a trauma hospital on the peninsula. She praises local firefighters and EMTs but says since Peninsula Hospital closed, response times have increased and trauma patients must be taken to Cohen's or Jamaica Hospital, making it harder for ambulances to return to the peninsula.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers raises need for trauma hospital on the Rockaway Peninsula

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I don't think me or the chair will be doing our job if we didn't bring up, like, the trauma hospital need on the peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I know it was mentioned that the response has been good comparatively to the city, which many of the firefighters live in our community, in my building, and all around, and EMT as well.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And we...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Value them and the work that they do.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But I'm always going to fight for more resources for both FDNY and EMT because what I hear on the ground has been that

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Particularly since Peninsula Hospital has closed several years ago, the response times have increased compared to what they once were.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: where we don't have an ambulance on the peninsula because if there's a trauma incident, they have to go out to Cohen's or to Jamaica Hospital and they get called in that area.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It takes even longer to come back to the peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I think for us, it's important to hear because when we talk about the trauma hospital, we're talking about

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: stopping the bleeding, trying to save a life.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But there are other important components to even getting to the hospital, and that includes often your division, your part of the city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so I would like to hear from you in terms of

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: how the city could better provide, like, work to address the need of the peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I know that's difficult for you to answer in your positions, but as truthfully as you can under oath.

chapters.summary: Maiano thanks the Council for supporting EMS and says he hears the committee's concerns. He describes a recent CAD change: when an ambulance leaves the peninsula for another hospital, it is placed in relocation status on the way back and only diverted to high-acuity calls like cardiac arrest, not low-acuity assignments.
chapters.title: Maiano thanks Council and describes ambulance redeployment changes

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So for EMS, if you just take one second before I answer that question, I just want to say that we as EMS, we hear...

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: The city council, we hear this committee and we appreciate you lobbying for us the way that you do.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We appreciate your help to get us a command car as well as other members of the council.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So that being said, you know, we hear it, we feel it, and we greatly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: As I said earlier,

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: With our Central Resource Coordination Center, right, we are consistently looking at areas where there are low ambulance availability and moving things throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: One thing that we have done within the last few months was we have what we call a redeployment.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: We changed the way we redeploy ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So now an ambulance that leaves the peninsula to go to another hospital, when they come available out of that other hospital, they are put in what's called a relocation status, and that allows them to get back to the peninsula,

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: and they do not get called for low-acuity assignments.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: They only get called if they are the closest ambulance to a high-acuity assignment like a cardiac arrest.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So that's one way that we are, besides the 24-hour center looking and redeploying units in, that is one way that we've made an improvement very recently to our CAD system to be able to, it's automatic.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: This is not something that has to be done by a person.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: It is automatic.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: They come available out of that hospital, and they are put on redirection back to that area.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says when larger incidents occur on the peninsula, resources are pulled from Howard Beach and Springfield Gardens, leaving those communities short. She asks whether staffing is why more personnel cannot be based on the peninsula; Maiano says EMS staffs to average call volume, while Sirocco says FDNY relocates and backfills units during fires.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks about resource thinning from nearby communities

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that update.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then also I've heard from like some of the other houses that when we have, I guess it may be like a three alarm that triggers like more support that's needed on the peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Like we're pulling from like Howard Beach.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We're pulling from Springfield Gardens, which then is leaving those community without their personnel.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is it a staffing issue why we don't have just more people located on the peninsula?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Like, how is that determined in terms of how many trucks, how many personnel are based there?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: Fire or EMS question?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Well, both can answer, really, because I've heard it from both that we drain, not to say drain, but we use other houses, resources when we have a certain level

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: happening on the peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So obviously I'll let Chief Sirocco speak about the fire side, but for EMS, right, we look at the average call volume in the particular area and we staff to try and meet that call volume.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So that's why we have 10 ambulances that's located on the peninsula.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Regarding fire operations, if there's a fire on the peninsula, obviously we'll relocate other units from other areas in there to cover possible other fire in that same area.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: And we do backfill those positions from other areas.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Obviously, we're spreading ourselves thinner out, but that's how we do it via the relocation process.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what the right number is so the peninsula is covered without feeling stretched. Sirocco says FDNY can handle multi-incident deployments by moving assets from other boroughs and notes that during the storm it added a fifth firefighter to peninsula engines and added a fifth engine on Cross Bay.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks what staffing level avoids stretching resources

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And that's the point I was getting to, like the thinning out piece.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So, like, what is that sweet number where...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It's sufficient, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Feeling like you're kind of stretched?

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Well, you know, I mean, obviously we can handle multi-incidents in our city the way we deploy our assets.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So we'll pull assets from other boroughs, you know, on targeted areas that we feel need coverage.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So I think our dispatchers alone, our chief of department, do a great job in reassigning assets.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: to locations to make sure they're properly covered.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: You know, for example, over the weekend, we also added some additional staffing during the storm.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: We added a fifth firefighter to all the engines on the peninsula because of, you know, it's isolated.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So we took care of that.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: We also added a fifth fire engine 331 on Cross Bay.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: Again, these additional staffing in case they were, you know, we were looking at the weather forecast that that would be possibly flooded.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So we wanted to be proactive in adding that additional staffing.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: So all those things combined, I think overall we do a pretty good job in moving our assets around to have substantial coverage in every area by backfilling the rockaways and bringing assets and spreading them out.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: I think we do a pretty good.

utterances.speaker: John Sirocco
utterances.text: The fifth firefighter is great during the flood area, and it does substantially help us.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They're great all the time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We would love to keep the fifth.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers acknowledges the administration's door-knocking in the Rockaways during the nor'easter but says infrastructure projects need to move faster. She says Rosedale and Brookville Park were badly flooded, requests NYCEM and DEP resources for Rosedale, and asks how much funding FRANK receives and how long its contract lasts.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers pivots to Rosedale flooding and FRANK funding

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'm going to end on this.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I do want to pivot to the Nor'easter that happened this weekend.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I acknowledge the administration for door knocking through the rockaways to be proactive.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I will say, which is not for you all, but on the record, I do feel like a lot of our infrastructure projects need to happen quicker

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: to be able to handle the current state of our climate impacts on the communities like the peninsula and the inland because we're seeing it more.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That leads me to Rosedale.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Rosedale took in a significant amount of water this weekend and damaged.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Brookville Park was completely underwater.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And there were a lot of homes that were deeply impacted by the storm.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know that there has been a focus on the coastal communities.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Primarily as we do need it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But I do want to ask NISM as well as, and I'll follow up on this, DEP to come into the community with some resources.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know you said you guys had delivered a number of

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: resources over the weekend, which was great, but Rosedale is requesting to have an event where they can also get like the flood centers and the pumps and all of those things too.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then my last question is, I know you're funding

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Frank in Far Rockaway.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I just wanted to understand how much is that funding and how long is that contract?

chapters.summary: Farrell says the nor'easter was mostly coastal but acknowledges Rosedale's summer flooding and says she will bring DEP town hall requests back to that agency. She says Strengthening Communities is funded for several years through Hurricane Ida disaster recovery money, with start-up, maintenance, and activation payments to networks like FRANK.
chapters.title: Farrell responds on Rosedale flooding, DEP town halls, and Strengthening Communities

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So all very good questions.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So for this weekend, you know, looking at the nor'easter, it was mostly coastal, but then we know what happened this summer.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And I know you were sending and your chief of staff was sending me the videos and the pictures of what was happening in Rosedale.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: DEP, I won't speak for them, but they have been doing the town halls, the flooding town halls.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so if there hasn't been...

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: been one in Rosedale in that area, we can bring that back to them.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I was at one in Hollis last week where they gave out about 150.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But we went nice in there too.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We come.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We go when they go.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I was there last week, and we're doing one in Forest Hills in a couple weeks with Councilwoman Shulman, and so I will bring that back.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: I will also say since emergency management is reporting to the deputy mayor for operations now and many of the agencies you mentioned, such as DEP, parks, fire, transportation, we all report in there.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, they have been.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: Looking at a lot of this infrastructure, that's the deputy mayor's background, is large infrastructure projects.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: You know, what can be pushed forward?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: What can we do in the interim?

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: All of that.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so, you know, definitely something we can follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And then your last question.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So for right now, Strengthening Communities is funded through the next several years.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: It's funded through disaster recovery money that the city received after Hurricane Ida.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: So it is stable for the next few years.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We are working with City Hall and OMB for how that program will be funded when that disaster funding is concluded.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And so we fund, the model is that we fund when networks join, we give them, you know, several thousand dollars to build their plan, to train their staff, to bring in their partners.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And then there is maintenance funding to keep that up.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And then the model is that we will activate them and pay them for that activation when they do the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: We did that several times during the winter weather in January and February.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And I will give all the networks a shout out that they actually were out putting up flyers through those extremely cold

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: temperatures in subway stations, in bodegas, liquor stores, laundromats, houses of worship, anywhere where people might have gone that needed assistance, needed a warm place.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: They did the same thing in the reverse over July 4th weekend because when it was so hot, getting people into cooling centers and other safe locations.

utterances.speaker: Christina Farrell
utterances.text: And then this weekend, we looked specifically at coastal areas, and we are able to activate them and then pay them for their effort.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says the previous administration committed to updating the Rockaway Peninsula evacuation route, but roads have changed, some have been demapped, development has altered the footprint, signs are missing, and new residents do not know where to go. She asks NYCEM and the Chair what steps are needed to begin updating the route.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks how to update the Rockaway evacuation route

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And my last, last, last question.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Evacuation route.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The last administration, I have a letter committed to updating the evacuation route for the Rockaway Peninsula.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Obviously, the roads have changed.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Some roads have been demapped now.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The footprint looks different because of all of the development.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We have a lot of new people on the peninsula also that don't know what even the current evacuation route is.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The signs are down, so they're not up on the poles anymore in many instances, and no one knows where to go in those moments.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I like to begin.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: to explore with the chair and NISM, what are the steps that are actually needed to update the evacuation route so that we can start that process?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know the community board has followed up on this as well, but we did get a letter committed to that based on some of the ULARP actions that we took.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But again, the reality is some of these roads that once were probably a part of this evacuation route don't exist anymore.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Like next door, they just renamed Edgemere Avenue because it's now located somewhere different now.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So we want to make sure everything is up to date.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But again, thank you, Chair, and thank you all for helping with this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know we have some follow-ups.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Of course.

chapters.summary: Chair Ariola thanks Brooks-Powers for her questions and says she raised powerful issues. She notes Council Member Sanchez had to leave but wanted to thank NYCEM, FDNY, and all agencies for a strong interagency response at 1484 Montgomery.
chapters.title: Chair Ariola thanks Brooks-Powers and relays Sanchez's praise for interagency response

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You brought up some very powerful and compelling issues and questions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So Councilmember Sanchez was here earlier, but she had to leave.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But she wanted me to thank NISM and FDMY and all the agencies for a really great interagency response to 1484 Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I wanted to put that on the record.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks when EMS last experienced a sustained service level below 25% for over 24 hours. Maiano says it was during COVID, and Ariola says that was a long time ago and she considers the current situation a state of emergency.
chapters.title: Ariola asks when EMS last had sustained service below 25%

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to get back to with EMS about the sustained levels.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So when was the last time there was a sustained level of under 25% for over 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: COVID.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: It was during the COVID period of time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right, when nobody was out.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, and you were only going for COVID.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So that was a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So we've had over for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I consider that a state of emergency.

chapters.summary: Ariola says road designs in Rockaway have changed without notifying firehouses and EMS stations, citing an ambulance station 11 minutes from Scholars Academy and delays reaching emergencies. Maiano says ambulances are dynamic and deployed on cross streets rather than fixed stations, while Sirocco says FDNY works with DOT and local units to review road changes for apparatus access.
chapters.title: Ariola asks how road redesigns affect emergency access in Rockaway

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The council member brought up the difference is in the road designs over the last number of years.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So in Rockaway, there is an ambulance station 11 minutes away by a regular car ride to the Scholars Academy.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It's a middle school and a high school.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Emergency vehicles often get delayed in the area because of road design that has occurred without notification.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: to the firehouses, to the EMS stations, and how much of an impact does that have on you being able to reach a fire or someone who's sick

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: when you're getting there and all of a sudden the road has been reconfigured and you can no longer go down that road?

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: So differently than how the fire responds, ambulances don't stay at one location, like the ambulance station.

utterances.speaker: Paul Maiano
utterances.text: Those 10 ambulances that come out of the rockways out of every station are deployed on cross streets throughout the city.

summary: The Committee on Fire and Emergency Management held an oversight hearing on emergency response in the Rockaways and other geographically isolated NYC communities, focusing on the July 25 Far Rockaway fire/homicide and the late-September nor'easter.

NYCEM Commissioner Christina Farrell, FDNY EMS Chief Paul Maiano, and Assistant Chief John Sirocco testified on response protocols, staffing, evacuation zones, Red Cross hotel placement, and EMS dispatch failures.

Council Members Brooks-Powers and Ariola pressed agencies on response times, EMS staffing and retention, trauma support for displaced families, evacuation routes, and the need for a Rockaway trauma hospital; public witnesses also testified on FDNY CAD systems and Rockaway infrastructure.
